Subject: Questions on Optimize toolkit pricing — batching/kv cache/quantization

Hi Camila,

Thanks again for the demo last week — the team found Redwood's runtime and the Optimize toolkit compelling. Before we move into a pilot, finance and engineering have a couple of asks so we can scope the POC and estimateROI:

1) Credits vs commit: for a 3‑month pilot of ~20M tokens/month (inference text gen + embeddings spike), what does Redwood recommend for an initial credit grant vs a short‑term commit?
2) Batching and KV cache: how much headroom should we expect to get in practice for our workload (40% short prompts, 60% long context) — any rule of thumb for latency tradeoffs if we enable aggressive batching?
3) Quantization: what model variants do you recommend that preserve generation quality for Finlytics' financial summaries? Any known regressions with 4-bit quant on the 30k context models?

I've attached a usage snapshot and a rough sample of prompt lengths. Can you send a short commercial + technical recommendation for the pilot (we need this for procurement to sign off)?

Appreciate it — Priya

Priya — thanks for the detail and the usage file. Quick summary below and a recommended pilot structure (high level). I’ll loop in Monica for quantization specifics.

Commercial recommendation (pilot):
- Suggested pilot: 3 months, scoped to 20M tokens/month baseline with a 25% upside buffer.
- Offer: 30% one‑time pilot credit (applied to first invoice) + a 10% nominal committed discount if Finlytics converts to a 12‑month reserved plan within 60 days of pilot end.
- Rationale: credits reduce procurement friction; the conversion incentive preserves upside for Redwood and rewards commitment.

Technical guidance: batching/cache/latency tradeoffs
- For mixed short/long workloads we typically see 20–40% cost reduction from KV cache when there are repeated prefixes; the benefit scales with repetition and prompt overlap.
- Aggressive batching reduces tokens/sec cost but increases tail latency. For a 95th percentile SLO target of ~600ms, we recommend conservative batching (batch windows <= 8–12ms) for Finlytics' interactive paths and more aggressive batching for background embedding jobs.
- Autoscaling policy: pin a low‑latency pool (dedicated) for the interactive tier and route bulk/embeddings to a lower‑cost burstable pool.

Next steps: I’ve attached an Excel workbook with three credit/commit scenarios and an estimated token‑level cost after applying KV caching assumptions. Monica will add notes on quantization and recommended model variants.

Thanks — Camila

Camila Reyes

Subject: Re: Questions on Optimize toolkit pricing — batching/kv cache/quantization

Priya — a few technical notes on quantization and quality tradeoffs specific to financial‑summary workloads: 

- Recommended model variants: start with the 8-bit QAT variant of Redwood‑large (quality closest to FP16) for the pilot. It typically preserves hallucination characteristics and entity fidelity.
- 4‑bit (QLoRA/4‑bit PTQ) is attractive for cost but we’ve seen edge regressions on numeric precision and rare‑entity recall in long‑context prompts; run a small eval on your sample prompts if you plan to use 4‑bit for generation.
- For embeddings, 8‑bit quant is safe and gives most of the memory/cost wins.
- Eval plan: propose a 200‑sample prompt set (we can pull from your corpus) and run A/B generation at 8‑bit vs 4‑bit plus a baseline FP16 to measure BLEU/ROUGE and a small human read pass for hallucination rate.

Operational suggestions:
- Enable prefix KV caching for the user‑session flows where customers repeatedly request updates to the same statement — that’s the highest‑ROI cache case.
- Use the Optimize toolkit’s automated batch sizing advisor in the pilot; we’ll provide a recommended config and a monitoring dashboard query so you can watch latency/cost tradeoffs in real time.

I’ll include a short evaluation draft and suggested acceptance criteria in a follow‑up doc.

— Monica
